meta.title: Claude Opus 5.5 · Materials science · solo · run 1
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 3 of 7 credited claims; 3 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Extended composition features + LightGBM/ExtraTrees with metal gate cut expt_gap MAE 28% vs baseline
artifacts.summary: Features: all 26 Magpie element properties (weighted mean, mean abs dev, min, max, range, majority-element value), L_p stoichiometry norms, valence-orbital fractions, raw element fractions. Model: average of LightGBM (L1 objective) and ExtraTrees regressors; a LightGBM classifier for gap==0 sets predicted metals to exactly 0 and clips negatives. 5-fold CV on public train (same folds for both): baseline MAE 0.471 eV vs 0.339 eV, winning 5/5 folds.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.1036, 95% CI [-0.1325, -0.0764], beyond the minimum effect 0.0084)

claim.statement: On expt_gap, the extended-feature LightGBM+ExtraTrees ensemble with a metal/non-metal gate achieves lower MAE than the reference Magpie-lite gradient-boosting baseline (5-fold CV MAE 0.339 vs 0.471 eV).

artifacts.title: Extended composition features + LightGBM/ExtraTrees cut steels yield-strength MAE 23% vs baseline
artifacts.summary: Features: all 26 Magpie element properties (weighted mean, mean abs dev, min, max, range, majority-element value), L_p stoichiometry norms, valence-orbital fractions, raw element fractions. Model: average of LightGBM and ExtraTrees. Raw element fractions matter most here since steels are near-identical in averaged properties. 5-fold CV, same folds: baseline 130.0 MPa vs 99.5 MPa, 5/5 folds won. Small dataset (240 public rows), so hidden-set variance is high.

artifacts.title: Raw element-fraction features are the main driver of the steels gain (ablation)
artifacts.summary: Same LightGBM+ExtraTrees ensemble and extended Magpie statistics, with vs. without the 103 raw element-fraction features. 5-fold CV (identical folds): with fractions 99.5 MPa MAE, without 106.7 MPa; with-fractions arm wins 5/5 folds. On expt_gap the same ablation gives only 0.008 eV (4/5 folds) and on glass 0.001 (3/5), so fractions matter specifically for the compositionally narrow steels family where averaged properties barely vary.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -12.7880, 95% CI [-22.1364, -5.0183], beyond the minimum effect 2.0700)

claim.statement: On steels, adding raw element-fraction features to extended Magpie statistics lowers yield-strength MAE (5-fold CV 99.5 vs 106.7 MPa, 5/5 folds).

artifacts.title: Hurdle model (regressor trained on non-metals only) lowers expt_gap MAE vs single regressor + gate
artifacts.summary: Arm a: classifier (LightGBM+ExtraTrees avg) for gap==0, and a regressor (LightGBM L1 + ExtraTrees) trained only on non-metal rows; predict 0 if P(metal)>0.5. At evaluation, compositions whose metal/non-metal label is public in expt_is_metal/train.csv override the gate (cross-dataset lookup). Arm b: the published v1 model (findin-5aa232e2), where the regressor is trained on all rows including zeros. 5-fold CV with no lookup: 0.323 vs 0.339 eV MAE, but arm a wins only 3/5 folds, so the gain is modest. Caveat: in CV the lookup gain grows with the fraction of test labels revealed (0.317 at 5%, 0.310 at 10%). However, the public expt_is_metal compositions absent from gap train are 99.6% non-metals, so on hidden data the lookup can only fix false-metal gate errors, and the realistic benefit is smaller than the CV simulation suggests.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0037, 95% CI [-0.0237, 0.0177], needed below -0.0063

claim.statement: On expt_gap, a hurdle model whose gap regressor is trained only on non-metals achieves lower MAE than the same features with a regressor trained on all compounds (5-fold CV MAE 0.323 vs 0.339 eV).

relations.reason: the extension itself is not an accepted contribution

artifacts.title: Negative results: kNN stacking, mismatch descriptors, extra metal labels did not help
artifacts.summary: All on identical 5-fold CV splits vs the published LightGBM+ExtraTrees model. (1) Adding a distance-weighted 5-NN on element fractions to the ensemble: glass 0.1139 vs 0.1099 error (0/5 folds), expt_is_metal 0.0855 vs 0.0828 (1/5) [exec-1026e29e, exec-79076911]. (2) Hume-Rothery-style mismatch descriptors (size delta, electronegativity, valence, melting-T, mass) + 3-seed LightGBM averaging: glass 0.1121 vs 0.1099 (1/5), expt_is_metal 0.0825 vs 0.0828 (1/5) [exec-03366fab, exec-6c4337f3]; the property min/max/range/deviation statistics already encode this information. (3) Training the expt_gap metal gate with the 237 extra expt_is_metal compositions: 0.331 vs 0.323 eV MAE for the hurdle model without them [exec-cc84ca68]; these extras are 99.6% non-metals, so they mostly shift the gate's class balance. Not preregistered, so reported as a note rather than null results.
artifacts.reason: not credited: notes are never credited

artifacts.title: Replication over 3 new CV seeds: expt_is_metal gain over baseline holds in 14/15 folds
artifacts.summary: Same model and code as findin-fcc2af49, re-scored on 15 folds from three different KFold seeds (1, 2, 3; seed 0 was used originally). Baseline error rate 0.0925 vs model 0.0793 (14.3% relative), and the model wins 14 of 15 folds with no ties. The original single-split result (3/5 folds) understated how consistent the gain is. The same check on glass (exec-fda6ca52) gives 0.1219 vs 0.1131 (7.2%), with 10 wins, 1 tie and 4 losses out of 15, so the glass gain is real but noisier.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0098, 95% CI [-0.0196, -0.0008], needed below -0.0015

events.text: Start by reading the guide and data layout.

```bash
sed -n 40,200p /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py; lab schema; cat /lab/data/GUIDE.md | head -60; for d in expt_gap expt_is_metal glass steels; do cat /lab/data/$d/meta.json; head -3 /lab/data/$d/train.csv; wc -l /lab/data/$d/train.csv; done
```
Check available libraries and data overlaps (duplicates, cross-dataset composition overlap), which shape strategy.

Every expt_gap composition also appears in expt_is_metal with consistent labels; useful for cross-task features. Let me look at element properties, then build a stronger featurizer + LightGBM pipeline and compare against the baseline in CV on all datasets.

Plan: one script with a richer featurizer (all 26 element properties, more statistics, raw element fractions) feeding a LightGBM + ExtraTrees ensemble. It scores the reference baseline and my model on the same 5-fold CV for every dataset.

```bash
mkdir -p /work/exp1 && cd /work/exp1 && cp /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py . && cat > run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, json, numpy as np, pandas as pd, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
from materials_baseline import parse_formula, baseline_predict
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.ensemble impor
A stray tag on the last line made bash reject the whole block, so nothing was written. Re-running it cleanly, with the local runs in the background writing to logs.

No local runs happened: all four died on import, so I have no results yet. Checking whether the `cp` of the baseline module actually landed in the directory.

```bash
cd /work/exp1; ls -la; ls -la /lab/data/baselines/
```

Both files are there, so the import should have resolved; it may have been a timing issue with the background launch. Rerunning with an explicit `PYTHONPATH` to rule out path resolution.

```bash
cd /work/exp1; for d in steels glass expt_gap expt_is_metal; do nohup env PYTHONPATH=/work/exp1 DATA_DIR=/lab/data OUT_DIR=/tmp python /work/exp1/run.py $d > /tmp/local_$d.log 2>&1 & done; sleep 90; tail -n 3 /tmp/local_*.log
```

Logs are still empty, so all four runs are still going with no results yet. Waiting before launching anything else, so I don't oversubscribe the 16 CPUs.

```bash
sleep 150; tail -n 3 /tmp/local_*.log; uptime
```

Load average is 0.00 even though four supposedly running jobs should be using CPU, and the logs are empty. The background processes are probably being killed when the command block returns. Checking `ps` before deciding how to run.

```bash
ps aux | grep run.py | grep -v grep | head; cd /work/exp1 && timeout 120 env DATA_DIR=/lab/data OUT_DIR=/tmp python run.py steels; echo exit $?
```

The four background jobs are in fact running, about 7 CPU-minutes each; the 0.00 load average was misleading. The foreground run failed on the import without `PYTHONPATH`, which suggests the script's own directory isn't on `sys.path` here (perhaps `PYTHONSAFEPATH` is set). `lab exec` might behave the same way, so I'll make `run.py` add its own directory to the path explicitly.

```bash
env | grep -i python; cd /work/exp1 && sed -i '1a import sys as _s, os as _o; _s.path.insert(0, _o.path.dirname(_o.path.abspath(__file__)))' run.py && head -3 run.py; sleep 60; tail -n 2 /tmp/local_*.log
```

`PYTHONSAFEPATH=1` is set, which explains the import failure. `run.py` now adds its own directory to `sys.path`, so `lab exec` should be safe. The four local CV jobs are still running with no results yet; I'll wait for them rather than start more jobs on the same CPUs.

```bash
sleep 180; tail -n 2 /tmp/local_*.log; lab budget
```

On local 5-fold CV (not yet recorded, so not evidence), the ensemble beats the baseline on three datasets so far. `expt_gap` is still running.

| Dataset | Baseline CV error | Model CV error | Relative improvement | Folds won |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| steels (MAE, MPa) | 130.0 | 99.5 | 23.5% | 5/5 |
| expt_is_metal (error rate) | 0.0928 | 0.0828 | 10.8% | 3/5 |
| glass (error rate) | 0.1168 | 0.1099 | 5.9% | 5/5 |

Four findings are published, all passing live checks. The two weakest are glass (0.7-point gain) and expt_is_metal (3/5 folds), so I'll spend the remaining time on two questions:
1. **Ablation:** how much of the gain comes from the raw element-fraction features versus the extended property statistics?
2. **Nearest neighbours:** many glass alloys share a chemical system and differ only in ratios. Adding a nearest-neighbour model on element fractions to the ensemble might help there.

I'll build `run2.py` with switchable variants and CV-score them on identical folds.

```bash

The ablation shows the raw element fractions matter most for steels: removing them costs 7.2 MPa MAE and loses 5/5 folds. They help less on expt_gap (0.008 eV, 4/5 folds) and barely at all on glass. Adding a kNN model to the ensemble made both glass and expt_is_metal worse, so I'm dropping that idea.

Next target is expt_gap, where the public data offers two levers:
1. **Hurdle model:** fit the regressor only on non-metals, with a gate predicting metals as 0.
2. **Cross-dataset metal labels:** the expt_is_metal train set contains about 237 compositions absent from gap train, which are likely i

Published the steels ablation as a comparison finding (findin-ca1e221f). The expt_gap hurdle/cross-dataset experiment is running. One caveat on the lookup arm: the 20% reveal rate in CV is my assumption about how much of the hidden gap set overlaps the public expt_is_metal labels. I haven't verified it, so any claim from that arm needs that caveat.

```bash
sleep 200; grep -E 'exec_id|stdout|Error' /tmp/exp3.log | head -4
```

The expt_gap experiment log is still empty after 200 s, so there are no results yet. It fits four variants per fold, so it should take a few minutes more; checking again.

```bash
sleep 150; cat /tmp/exp3.log | grep -E 'exec_id|stdout|rror' | head -5; ps aux | grep run3 | grep -v grep | wc -l
```

The recorded CV run (exec-cc84ca68) on expt_gap gives:

| Variant | CV MAE (eV) | Folds won vs v1 |
|---|---|---|
| v1 (published model) | 0.339 | — |
| hurdle (regressor fit only on non-metals) | 0.323 | 3/5 |
| hurdle + extra metal labels in the gate | 0.331 | 2/5 |
| hurdle + metal labels + lookup at 20% reveal | 0.297 | 5/5 |

The extra metal labels did not help the gate, and the lookup gain depends on my assumed 20% reveal rate. At most 237 hidden-gap compositions can be looked up (about 21% of 1144), and likely fewer.

To isolate that effect cleanly, `run4.py` compares hurdle+lookup with

The ids are not ordered by composition, so they give no hint about overlap. The more important result: of the 237 expt_is_metal compositions absent from gap train, only 0.4% are metals, so roughly 1 of them. Any lookup hits on the hidden gap set would therefore almost all say "non-metal". That only helps by stopping the gate from wrongly zeroing a true non-metal, and it never sets a metal's prediction to 0. My CV simulation revealed a random mix of metals and non-metals, so it overstates the lookup gain. Any claim must rest mainly on the hurdle itself, with reveal fraction 0. Waiting for exp4.

On expt_gap, fitting the regressor only on non-metals with no lookup cuts CV MAE from 0.339 to 0.323 eV, but wins only 3/5 folds. The bigger lookup gains come from a CV simulation that reveals true metals, which the hidden data will rarely offer. So I'll claim only the 0.323 vs 0.339 hurdle result and state those caveats. The hurdle result is published as findin-40efc896, though the smoke test overstates the lookup: all 40 test rows were hits because they came from train. The hidden-set hit rate will be far lower.

- **Seed averaging:** average LightGBM over 3

The mismatch features and seed averaging did not help. On glass they made things worse: 0.1121 vs 0.1099 error rate, winning only 1/5 folds. On expt_is_metal the gain was negligible: 0.0825 vs 0.0828, also 1/5 folds. A formal null result would need a preregistration made before these runs, which I don't have.
